intro: Case studies of participation, petition and budgeting programs elsewhere: what happened, what evaluators found, and the limits. Each cites its sources.

cases.title: The New England town meeting
cases.what_happened: For nearly four centuries, hundreds of New England towns have governed themselves by open meeting: any resident may attend, speak, and vote directly on budgets, bylaws, and local decisions.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Durability. Town meetings survived the printing press, the telegraph, and the internet. Visiting in 1831, Alexis de Tocqueville wrote that New England town governments showed greater political independence than any municipal body he knew in Europe — he called town institutions the schools where liberty is learned.
cases.caveats: Attendance in modern town meetings has declined with town size — the same scale limit Switzerland shows.

sources.label: Town meeting — history
Britannica: direct democracy

cases.title: Switzerland — voting as a habit
cases.what_happened: Swiss citizens vote on roughly 15 substantive questions a year, at every level of government. More than a third of all national referendums ever held on Earth took place in Switzerland. In thousands of small communes, citizens still assemble to pass budgets directly.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Direct participation can be a routine of civic life rather than a crisis instrument. Research on Swiss municipalities finds assembly attendance and turnout are strongest in smaller communes and decline as municipal size grows.
cases.caveats: Swiss referendums are binding under Swiss constitutional rules.

sources.label: The way to modern direct democracy in Switzerland
Direct democracy at the local level in Switzerland (research)

cases.title: vTaiwan — an open opinion-mapping process
cases.what_happened: Taiwan's government adopted an open process where citizens respond to statements — agree, disagree, pass — but can never reply to each other. Clustering software maps the opinion groups and surfaces statements that win support across them. The process reached 200,000 participants and produced real regulation: ride-sharing rules, online alcohol sales, revenge-porn law.
cases.what_evidence_shows: The Participedia case study reports that participants found areas of agreement across opinion groups on several topics. Participants could not reply to each other, and wrote statements they hoped would win support across groups.
cases.caveats: The Taiwanese government committed in advance to act on the results.

sources.label: vTaiwan — Participedia case study
Polis — the method

cases.title: Porto Alegre — participatory budgeting
cases.what_happened: The city that invented participatory budgeting let neighborhood assemblies rank capital spending priorities. Tens of thousands of residents — disproportionately poor residents — decided real allocations year after year.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Roads, water connections, and school access measurably improved in underserved districts; government responsiveness and civic organization strengthened; residents who participated became more politically active afterward. Later, when political commitment faded in the 2000s, the gains eroded.
cases.caveats: Porto Alegre allocated binding budget shares.

sources.label: WRI: Porto Alegre and the challenge of sustaining change
Participatory budgeting in Brazil (SDG16+)

cases.title: Better Reykjavik — half a city, one website
cases.what_happened: An open idea-and-debate platform where residents propose and argue for city improvements — with arguments for and against listed separately, never threaded. The city council committed to review the top ideas every month and publicly answer whether each was approved.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Over 70,000 participants out of 120,000 residents, with 30,000 registered users submitting 10,000 ideas (Citizens Foundation).
cases.caveats: These figures reflect a platform that has run since 2010.

sources.label: Better Reykjavik — Citizens Foundation
Better Reykjavik — Participedia

cases.title: Decidim — infrastructure that spread
cases.place: Barcelona, Spain — then hundreds of institutions
cases.what_happened: Barcelona built an open-source participation platform — proposals, budgets, assemblies, consultations — and released the software publicly. 25,000 residents signed up in its first two months and submitted over 10,000 proposals shaping the city's action plan.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Decidim runs hundreds of instances across Europe, from small towns to regional governments, each with its own configuration.
cases.caveats: Decidim was built with a large city’s budget.

sources.label: Decidim Barcelona — city council
Decidim participatory budgeting — Participedia

cases.title: Deliberative polling — what happens to people who participate
cases.what_happened: James Fishkin's method: gather a random sample, give them balanced briefing materials and moderated small-group discussion, measure opinions before and after. It has run over a hundred times across dozens of countries.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Participants gain measurable knowledge, and a single deliberative weekend produced large effects on civic engagement and voting nearly a year later (Stanford FSI). Participants came to follow politics more closely and to see their own opinions as worth having. Shifts in specific policy views often faded with time; the engagement effects lasted.
cases.caveats: Deliberative polls use random samples and paid weekends; participants are not self-selected.

sources.label: Stanford FSI: lasting effects of deliberation
Can deliberation have lasting effects? (APSR)

cases.title: Lahti — voting at the library
cases.what_happened: City-wide participatory budgeting where residents proposed ideas and voted on allocations — and, critically, anyone could vote in person at the public libraries, not just online.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Per People Powered, in-person voting at the public libraries reached residents that online-only voting did not, and the participatory budget doubled the following year.
cases.caveats: Lahti’s program was funded by the municipality.

sources.label: People Powered: participatory budgeting and participation

cases.title: Washington County, Wisconsin — a small county moves real money
cases.what_happened: County Executive Josh Schoemann led a priority-based budgeting process that reallocated 15% of the county's entire operating budget according to articulated priorities.
cases.what_evidence_shows: According to the Center for Priority Based Budgeting, the county reallocated funds across programs according to its stated priorities.
cases.caveats: The process was led by the county executive’s office.

sources.label: Center for Priority Based Budgeting — county cases

cases.title: UK Parliament petitions — traction that guarantees an answer
cases.what_happened: Parliament’s petition site lets any citizen post a petition. At 10,000 signatures the government is obligated to publish a response; at 100,000 the Petitions Committee considers it for a parliamentary debate.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Millions of people have signed petitions on the site. The thresholds tie a number of signatures to a published response with a date and a record — even when the government’s answer is no, the answer exists in public.
cases.caveats: The thresholds are set by Parliament’s own rules.

sources.label: How petitions work — UK Parliament

cases.title: Tupelo, Mississippi — community development councils
cases.what_happened: In the 1940s, Lee County was among the poorest counties in the nation's poorest state. A local newspaper publisher, George McLean, organized what became the Tupelo model: seventeen businessmen staked a dairy program, the Community Development Foundation formed in 1948 to recruit industry, and — the distinctive move — rural community development councils brought farm families and townspeople into the same rooms to solve shared problems, decade after decade.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Lee County rose from the state’s poorest ranks to among its most affluent, building traditions of interracial cooperation and civic giving that community development scholars still study as ‘the Tupelo miracle.’
cases.caveats: Tupelo’s rise took about forty years.

sources.label: Mississippi Encyclopedia — the Tupelo Miracle
Mississippi Encyclopedia — George McLean

cases.title: Chattanooga — from dirtiest city to National Park City, starting with 1,700 residents
cases.what_happened: In 1969 the federal government named Chattanooga the worst city in America for particulate air pollution — nylon stockings reportedly disintegrated outdoors. The city passed its air ordinance within months and reached full industrial compliance by 1972. Then in 1984 came the deeper turn: Vision 2000, a community visioning process where about 1,700 residents proposed and voted on 2,500 ideas, distilled to 40 public goals.
cases.what_evidence_shows: By 1992, Vision 2000 had produced 223 implemented programs and projects — the Tennessee Aquarium and riverfront revival most famously. Four decades on, Chattanooga is North America’s first National Park City, with a municipal fiber network and an outdoor economy. Residents at large, rather than an appointed committee, proposed and voted on the goals.
cases.caveats: Chattanooga had foundation funding (Lyndhurst) and a metropolitan-scale budget.

cases.title: The Promise towns — Kalamazoo, El Dorado, and Arkadelphia itself
cases.place: Kalamazoo, MI · El Dorado, AR · Arkadelphia, AR
cases.what_happened: In 2005 anonymous donors promised every Kalamazoo public school graduate free in-state college tuition. Murphy Oil brought the model to El Dorado, Arkansas in 2007. And in 2010 the Ross Foundation and Southern Bancorp brought it home: the Arkadelphia Promise has awarded more than $1.17 million to Arkadelphia High graduates.
cases.what_evidence_shows: The Upjohn Institute's long-run research on Kalamazoo: four-year college enrollment up 34%, credential completion up from 36% to 48% of eligible graduates, low-income completion up more than 50%, and district enrollment grew 26% while peer districts shrank — a scholarship that changed a town's population curve. El Dorado's eligible graduates' college attendance rose from about 60% to over 80%. Arkadelphia’s own numbers, per the Arkadelphia Promise (listed in the sources below): the Class of 2011 was the first Promise class; within four graduating classes the program had funded 718 college semesters; 44% of recipients start at Henderson State and 14% at Ouachita Baptist; and the first class’s freshman-to-sophomore retention was 70%, compared with the Arkansas average of 61.4%.
cases.caveats: Promise programs need durable funders — El Dorado's outlived Murphy Oil's headquarters, but the dependence is real. And scholarships lift trajectories over decades, not budget cycles.

sources.label: Upjohn Institute — the Kalamazoo Promise at 16: outcomes

cases.title: California’s propositions — criticisms and defenses
cases.what_happened: California’s binding statewide initiative system lets anyone with enough signatures put a proposed law directly on the ballot. Critics cite a paid-signature industry, drafting without legislative compromise, voter fatigue across dozens of complex measures, and campaign spending.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Scholars note that initiative drafting does not incorporate the compromise that legislative debate requires. California Proposition 8 (2008) amended the state constitution to define marriage as between a man and a woman; a federal court ruled it unconstitutional in 2010, and the U.S. Supreme Court left that ruling in place in Hollingsworth v. Perry (2013). Other studies find voter-competence concerns overstated, and mass electorates harder for special interests to lobby than legislators are.
cases.caveats: Supporters note that the system has repeatedly put issues on the ballot that legislators had not taken up.
